## D Loss-Term Ablation

## D Loss-Term Ablation

We train LiLiCorr twice, with and without the distractor penalty of Eq. (4), holding everything else fixed. The two arms share the architecture, every other setting, and the total weight of the reranker objective, so removing the penalty hands its budget to the hard cross-entropy rather than shrinking the objective. Table 15 gives the per-benchmark acceptance lengths at concurrency one. The penalty raises acceptance length on all nine benchmarks, by 1.5% on the average, most on HumanEval at 3.8% and least on AlpacaEval at 0.2%. It is what trains the reranker against the candidates that actually cost acceptances rather than against the ground-truth label alone, and Appendix E derives it as an expected target cost.

## E Derivations for the Reranker Objective

The distractor penalty is an expected target cost. Write $P_{\theta}(k)$ for $P_{\theta} ( c_{s}=k \mid c_{s-1}=g_{s-1})$ , let $c_{k}=-\log q_{k}$ be the cost the target assigns to candidate k, low where the target is confident, and let $w_{k}=\mathrm{ReLU} ( c_{k}-c_{g_{s}} )$ be that cost relative to the ground truth after rectification. The penalty of Eq. (4) is then $\Omega_{s}=\sum_{k} P_{\theta}(k) w_{k}$ , the expected rectified cost of the candidate LiLiCorr commits to. When $g_{s}$ is the target's preferred candidate in the pool no cost is negative, the rectifier is inactive, and since $\sum_{k} P_{\theta}(k)=1$

$$
\Omega_ {s} = \sum_ {k} P _ {\theta} (k) \left(c _ {k} - c _ {g _ {s}}\right) = H \left(P _ {\theta}, q\right) - c _ {g _ {s}}, \quad H \left(P _ {\theta}, q\right) = \sum_ {k} P _ {\theta} (k) c _ {k}.
$$

(8)

$H ( P_{\theta}, q )$ is the expected target cost under $P_{\theta}$ , and the offset $c_{g_{s}}$ does not depend on the LiLiCorr parameters, so $\nabla_{\theta} \Omega_{s}=\nabla_{\theta} H ( P_{\theta}, q )$ : the penalty and a cross-entropy against the target have the same gradient. The penalty involves the target only through cost differences, so it is unchanged if $q$ is renormalized over the pool.

Why this is not distribution matching. The target is frozen, so the costs $c_{k}$ are constants and $\Omega_{s}$ is linear in $P_{\theta}$ . A linear function on the probability simplex attains its minimum at a vertex, that is, at a distribution placing all of its mass on one candidate, and the minimizing vertex is the candidate of least cost. Under the assumption above that candidate is $g_{s}$ , so minimizing the penalty drives LiLiCorr to commit to the target's preferred candidate rather than to reproduce the target's distribution over the pool. Committing is what the verifier rewards, since a block is accepted on the tokens the target would itself emit and mass placed elsewhere is not recovered.

The rectifier. At the occasional slot where $g_{s}$ is not the target's preferred candidate, the rectifier clips the negative costs that would otherwise reward a candidate the target ranks above the supervised token. Such slots are rare, and arise from numerical differences between the offline generation of the supervision and the teacher-forced target pass used during training, rather than from a genuine target preference.

Complementary gradients. The hard cross-entropy and the distractor penalty act on the groundtruth logit $z_{g}$ through complementary gradients. For cross-entropy,

$$
\frac {\partial \mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {C E}}}{\partial z _ {g}} = P _ {\theta} (g) - 1,
$$

(9)

which remains strong when $P_{\theta}(g)$ is small, exactly the hardest mistakes. For the penalty,

$$
\frac {\partial \Omega_ {s}}{\partial z _ {q}} = - P _ {\theta} (g) \mathbb {E} _ {P _ {\theta}} [ w ],
$$

(10)

$$
\frac {\partial \Omega_ {s}}{\partial z _ {q}} = - P _ {\theta} (g) \mathbb {E} _ {P _ {\theta}} [ w ],
$$

(10)

which vanishes as $P_{\theta}(g)\rightarrow 0$ , so the penalty alone is weak precisely when the ground truth is badly misranked. It is also indifferent among candidates of zero cost, including target ties and candidates the target ranks above g , since the rectifier clips their costs to zero. Cross-entropy therefore robustly pulls the exact ground-truth token upward, while $\Omega_{s}$ preferentially pushes target-rejected confusers downward, so the penalty is best viewed as cost-aware shaping of cross-entropy rather than a replacement for it. Both terms are evaluated only on the oracle prefix and averaged over the same slots, so slots after the first coverage miss contribute to neither.

## F Greedy Selection Versus the Highest-Scoring Path

Sections 3.3 and 3.5 argue that prefix acceptance rewards a greedy left-to-right decode over a search for the best-scoring block. We test the decode rule in isolation, holding the trained model fixed and varying only the rule that selects a path through the candidate lattice.

Path selection. Let $c=(c_{1},\dots,c_{B-1})$ denote a path, where $c_{s}$ is the candidate committed at slot s and $c_{0}$ is the anchor. Since LiLiCorr couples only adjacent slots, a path scores as the sum of its matching terms,

$$

The greedy rule of Section 3.5 commits each slot to the best continuation of what precedes it and never revisits an earlier choice. The alternative is to return the path that maximizes g. Enumeration is infeasible, as the lattice holds $K^{B-1}$ paths, but the pairwise structure of Eq. (11) makes the exact maximizer reachable in $O(B K^{2})$ time by dynamic programming. Sweeping left to right, one records for each candidate the score of the best path ending there, then traces the stored predecessors back from the best final candidate. This is the Viterbi algorithm (Viterbi, 1967), a strictly stronger optimizer of g than the greedy walk.

Why the stronger optimizer is not the better one here. Under prefix acceptance every slot contributes only while all the slots before it have matched, so the early ones carry most of the expected acceptance length, and a block that loses its first slot gains nothing from the rest. Maximizing g targets the block as a whole, which is essentially the probability that the entire block survives verification. Giving up an early slot to raise the total is rational for that objective and self-defeating here, because the improved tail is never reached. The greedy walk instead maximizes the leading decision exactly, and each later one conditioned on what was committed.

Results. The comparison is between decode rules for one trained model, not between formulations: LiLiCorr is trained under the local objective of Eq. (2), so its path score is calibrated for the walk it was trained to take. What Table 16 shows is that this calibration is worth more than the stronger optimizer, at equal serving cost. The exact optimizer decodes worse. It lowers acceptance length on all nine benchmarks, by 0.84 to 4.46% and by 2.64% on average. Throughput follows, since the two rules are equally cheap to serve: each is a single fused kernel folded into the same captured draft graph, and the two rules run as consecutive cells of one allocation, where the block rate they sustain differs by at most 0.44% on any benchmark and by 0.06% on average. The stronger optimizer is therefore had for free and still accepts less. Its worst case is AIME 2025, though at 30 problems that split carries the direction rather than the magnitude; every other benchmark lies between $- 0.84\%$ and $- 3.43\%$ . The smallest effect is on HumanEval, which is also the smallest split and carries the largest block-rate excursion of the nine.
